articles.title: DPDPA vs GDPR: What Developers and Privacy Teams Should Know
articles.excerpt: Privacy requirements increasingly affect technical decisions. Data collection, application architecture, APIs, cloud services, databases, analytics platforms, identity systems, and third-party integra…
articles.body: Privacy requirements increasingly affect technical decisions. Data collection, application architecture, APIs, cloud services, databases, analytics platforms, identity systems, and third-party integrations can all influence how an organization processes personal information. For Indian technology companies, the DPDPA introduces an important domestic privacy framework. For businesses serving European users, GDPR may also apply. Although both regulations address personal data protection, they should not be treated as interchangeable. One important difference is the scope of data covered. DPDPA focuses on digital personal data, while GDPR has a broader concept of personal data and can cover certain manual processing activities.

articles.body: Cryptocurrency Recovery Services: What You Need to Know After a Crypto Scam Losing cryptocurrency can be a devastating experience. Whether funds were stolen from a wallet, sent to a fraudulent investment platform, or transferred as part of a cryptocurrency scam, victims often begin searching for cryptocurrency recovery services to understand what options may be available. However, choosing a legitimate service requires caution. Unfortunately, cryptocurrency victims can become targets of a second scam where criminals pretend to be recovery specialists and promise to return lost funds for an upfront payment. A responsible cryptocurrency investigation should focus on evidence, blockchain analysis, transaction tracing, and realistic expectations rather than guaranteed recovery.

articles.title: Squelchy: a small live wrapper for noisy commands
articles.excerpt: I built Squelchy to keep noisy commands from taking over the terminal. It shows a small live view while a process runs, then prints a bounded report with the real exit code and a command to recover th…
articles.body: I built Squelchy to keep noisy commands from taking over the terminal. It shows a small live view while a process runs, then prints a bounded report with the real exit code and a command to recover the raw output. What it keeps Squelchy starts a program with its argv directly, without passing arguments through a shell. Standard input stays attached to the current terminal. It saves standard output and standard error byte for byte in separate files. A combined file records the chunk arrival order the wrapper observes. Concurrent streams have no guaranteed cross-stream chronology. The preview parser uses a bounded line buffer and small tail and error rings. It decodes split UTF-8 for display, removes terminal escape sequences, and clips previews. The log files stay unchanged.

articles.title: 31 Years Later, One of the Most Disturbing Thrillers Ever Made Is Officially Free on Streaming
articles.excerpt: Forget the Eli Roth movie, this 1995 horror movie belongs in the pantheon of so-bad-it's-good classics.
articles.body: Released in 1995, Ice Cream Man is the type of so-bad-it's-good horror movie that rarely gets made in the post- Get Out era where the genre is taken much more seriously. Directed by pornographer Paul Norman, who hoped this was his pivot to kid-friendly horror flicks, Ice Cream Man is a movie where a deranged killer mixes up bugs, human remains, and ice cream and feeds it to children. It's also a movie that spends a remarkable amount of time showing us what shoes everyone is wearing, as per a sponsorship agreement with Converse that probably cost some poor sneaker executive his job. Norman may have wanted to escape X-rated film, but he wound up making one of the creepiest stories ever put on film.

The questions that keep an audience obsessing over a TV show from week to week can lose their power the moment we finally get some answers. Explain too little, and viewers feel frustrated. Explain too much, and you run the risk of deflating the entire story. There’s always the third option, however, which is to answer questions with details that generate even more questions. Instead of a mystery box, why not make it a nesting doll of secrets?

articles.title: People really hate AI, so why can’t they get enough?
articles.excerpt: Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he…
articles.body: Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company. We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.” “I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist,” I replied. It was a joke! I love my job. But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype , steered by zealots , inescapable . The CEO of Springboards and I are far from alone. Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now. On the one hand, public feelings are souring fast.

articles.title: Mapping the Gaps in NASA’s Return to the Moon, featuring Richard Spolzino
articles.excerpt: “I want to be able to look at a rocket launch and say, ‘I touched a piece of this.’” That’s how Richard Spolzino describes the thing he’s chasing. Not a title, not a specific mission, not even NASA it…
articles.body: “I want to be able to look at a rocket launch and say, ‘I touched a piece of this.’” That’s how Richard Spolzino describes the thing he’s chasing. Not a title, not a specific mission, not even NASA itself, just the ability to point at something real and know his work made it possible. At NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia, Spolzino works within Moon Base’s mission architecture and systems interoperability effort, helping identify what NASA still doesn’t know about the Moon and Mars, and making sure that missing information gets found before it becomes a problem. articles.title: An AI couldn’t beat humans at StarCraft, so it decided to cheat
articles.excerpt: StarSkirmish pits AI-made StarCraft-playing bots against one another, as well as against human-made bots. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were essentially tied as the best-performing AI-made…
articles.body: StarSkirmish pits AI-made StarCraft-playing bots against one another, as well as against human-made bots. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were essentially tied as the best-performing AI-made bots, but they couldn't top Stardust, the top-rated human-made bot. On Friday, GPT was facing off against Claude and the human-created bot Pluto, but according to Kotaku , it couldn't quite get an edge. So it resorted to a tactic that is becoming alarmingly common for modern AI models - it broke the rules . GPT-6 Astra went and downloaded Stardust, and started running that instead of its own bot.
